---
title: "The Income & Fairness Dataset"
subtitle: "Real Census data, the group gap, and the channel that leaks"
---



The fairness module runs on a different dataset: a **real** slice of US Census
data with a **protected attribute** (`sex`), a **target** to predict
(`income_high`), and **proxy features** that quietly carry the protected attribute
even after you drop it.  This page shows all three — and the one feature,
`occupation`, where the leak really hides.

---

## 1 · The Columns

::: {#tbl-credit-head .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
print(f"rows: {len(credit):,}")
print(credit.head().to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
rows: 30,000
 age  education_years  hours_per_week                  occupation       marital  sex  income_high
  62               13              40              Office & Admin       Married    1            1
  33               16              65                       Sales       Married    1            0
  33               16              40 Management/Business/Finance Never married    0            0
  46               14              40              Office & Admin       Widowed    0            1
  32               16              40 Education/Legal/Arts/Social       Married    1            1
```
:::
:::


| Column | Role | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `sex` | **protected** | the attribute we must not discriminate on (1 = male) |
| `income_high` | **target** | 1 if personal income > \$50k — what a model predicts |
| `occupation` | **proxy** (strong) | job family; heavily sex-segregated, so it *carries* `sex` |
| `education_years`, `hours_per_week` | proxies (weak) | numeric features, mildly tied to `sex` |
| `marital` | proxy (weak) | marital status |
| `age` | control | a feature essentially *un*correlated with `sex` |

## 2 · The Group Gap

The whole problem in one chart: high-income rates differ by group.  This gap is
real in the data and is what a fairness method must *not* simply reproduce.

::: {#cell-fig-gap .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
p_male = credit.sex.mean()                                   # P(sex = male)
p_high = credit.income_high.mean()                           # P(income_high)
g_male = credit[credit.sex == 1].income_high.mean()          # P(high | male)
g_female = credit[credit.sex == 0].income_high.mean()        # P(high | female)
# group gap = P(high | male) − P(high | female)  — the target↔attribute dependence

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))
axL.bar(["male", "high-income"], [p_male, p_high], color=[COOL, BAND])
axL.set_ylim(0, 1); axL.set_ylabel("fraction of sample")
axL.set_title("Overall marginals", fontsize=12); despine(axL)
for i, v in enumerate([p_male, p_high]):
    axL.text(i, v + 0.02, f"{v:.0%}", ha="center", fontsize=10)

axR.bar(["female", "male"], [g_female, g_male], color=[WARM, COOL])
axR.set_ylim(0, 1); axR.set_ylabel("P(high income)")
axR.set_title(f"The group gap: {g_male - g_female:+.0%}", fontsize=12)
despine(axR)
for i, v in enumerate([g_female, g_male]):
    axR.text(i, v + 0.02, f"{v:.0%}", ha="center", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Left: overall marginals — the sample is ~53% male and ~41% high-income. Right: the high-income rate splits by sex, 47% for men vs 35% for women — a 12-point group gap. That gap is the dependence between the target and the protected attribute.](06-the-credit-dataset_files/figure-html/fig-gap-output-1.png){#fig-gap width=1304 height=465}
:::
:::


## 3 · Where the Leak Hides

Now the subtle part.  Drop `sex` and look at the **obvious** numeric features —
age, education, hours worked.  They barely correlate with `sex`, so you might
conclude the data is nearly clean.

::: {#cell-fig-numeric-proxies .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
feats = ["age", "education_years", "hours_per_week"]
F: Float[Array, "n_rows n_feats"] = credit[feats].to_numpy().astype(float)   # numeric features
s: Float[Array, "n_rows"] = credit.sex.to_numpy().astype(float)              # the attribute

# ρ(feature, sex) = Cov(feature, sex) / (σ_feature · σ_sex)  — centre, then contract n
F_c: Float[Array, "n_rows n_feats"] = F - F.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
s_c: Float[Array, "n_rows"] = s - s.mean()
cov: Float[Array, "n_feats"] = einx.dot("n f, n -> f", F_c, s_c) / len(s)    # Cov(feature, sex)
var_f: Float[Array, "n_feats"] = einx.dot("n f, n f -> f", F_c, F_c) / len(s)   # Var(feature)
var_s = float((s_c * s_c).mean())                                           # Var(sex)
ρ = pd.Series(cov / np.sqrt(var_f * var_s), index=feats).sort_values()      # Pearson ρ
colors = [plotting.PALETTE["green"] if abs(v) < 0.1 else CRASH for v in ρ.values]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 2.8))
ax.barh(ρ.index, ρ.values, color=colors)
ax.axvline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("correlation with sex")
ax.set_title("The obvious features barely leak sex", fontsize=12)
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Correlation of the numeric features with sex. Age and education are essentially zero; hours-per-week is only mildly positive (men work slightly longer hours). On this evidence alone you would think dropping sex is enough.](06-the-credit-dataset_files/figure-html/fig-numeric-proxies-output-1.png){#fig-numeric-proxies width=992 height=321}
:::
:::


It is not enough.  The leak hides in **`occupation`**, which is heavily
sex-segregated — and which *also* predicts income.  A feature that carries both is
exactly how the gap sneaks back in.

::: {#cell-fig-occupation .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
SHORT = {
    "Management/Business/Finance": "Mgmt/Business/Finance",
    "Computing/Engineering/Science": "Computing/Eng/Science",
    "Education/Legal/Arts/Social": "Education/Legal/Arts",
    "Service (food/clean/care/protective)": "Service",
    "Blue-collar (build/repair/prod/transport)": "Blue-collar",
}
# per occupation g:  pct_male = P(male | g),  pct_high = P(high income | g)
agg = (credit.groupby("occupation")
       .agg(pct_male=("sex", "mean"), pct_high=("income_high", "mean"))
       .sort_values("pct_male"))
labels = [SHORT.get(t, t) for t in agg.index]
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.4), sharey=True)
axL.barh(labels, agg.pct_male * 100, color=COOL)
axL.axvline(50, color=INK, lw=1.2, ls="--")
axL.set_xlabel("% male"); axL.set_title("Occupation encodes sex", fontsize=12)
despine(axL)
axR.barh(labels, agg.pct_high * 100, color=BAND)
axR.set_xlabel("% high-income"); axR.set_title("…and encodes income", fontsize=12)
despine(axR)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Each occupation group's share of men (left) and its high-income rate (right), same order. Occupation runs from 25% male (Healthcare) to 82% (blue-collar) — so it encodes sex — and its income rate runs from 15% to 77% — so it encodes the target. A model leaning on occupation inherits both.](06-the-credit-dataset_files/figure-html/fig-occupation-output-1.png){#fig-occupation width=1304 height=513}
:::
:::


How much does occupation give away?  Guess each person's sex from their
occupation's majority alone — no other feature — and check the hit rate:

::: {#6579b617 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# proxy leak: guess sex from the occupation majority, score acc = mean(guess == sex)
occ_male = credit.groupby("occupation").sex.transform("mean")   # P(male | occupation)
guess_male = (occ_male > 0.5).astype(int)                       # predict the majority sex
acc = (guess_male == credit.sex).mean()                         # acc = mean(guess == sex)
baseline = max(credit.sex.mean(), 1 - credit.sex.mean())        # always-majority baseline
print(f"guess sex from occupation alone : {acc:.0%} correct")
print(f"baseline (always guess 'male')  : {baseline:.0%}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
guess sex from occupation alone : 65% correct
baseline (always guess 'male')  : 53%
```
:::
:::


Occupation alone recovers `sex` well above chance — so a model that scores income
on occupation is, in part, scoring on `sex`.  That is **proxy leakage**, and here
it is in real data, not a synthetic construction.

## 4 · Real Data, and How to Reproduce It

The table is the **ACSIncome** task from
[`folktables`](https://github.com/socialfoundations/folktables) — the modern,
fairness-focused successor to UCI Adult — built on the US Census **American
Community Survey**.  We take one large, diverse state (California, 2018 1-year),
apply the standard ACSIncome filter, decode the coded columns into readable
features, and sample a fixed 30,000-row panel.  Two steps deserve a closer look
before the script: the **decode** that turns Census numeric codes into the
readable columns above, and the **ACSIncome filter** that decides which survey
rows survive.

### 4a · The Decode — coded Census columns → readable features

The raw ACS row is a vector of integer **codes**, not words.  `SEX` is `1`/`2`,
income lives in `PINCP` as raw dollars, and the job is a four-digit Census
**OCCP** code.  The decode is a fixed lookup, drawn verbatim from
[`download_credit_data.py`](../../scripts/download_credit_data.py):

- **`SEX`** — `1` → male, `2` → female.  We store `sex = (SEX == 1)`, so the
  protected attribute becomes `1 = male`, `0 = female`.
- **`PINCP`** (personal income, dollars) — the **target** is the threshold
  `PINCP > 50000` → `income_high = 1`.  A single cut turns a dollar amount into
  the binary label a scorecard predicts.
- **`OCCP`** (occupation, ~500 SOC-derived codes) — collapsed by **code range**
  into readable families.  The script's `_OCC_RANGES` maps, e.g.,
  `10–960 → Management/Business/Finance`, `3000–3655 → Healthcare`,
  `6005–9760 → Blue-collar`.  Eight ranges in all; anything unmatched falls to
  `Military/Other`.

The page below illustrates the decode honestly with a tiny **hand-built**
coded → readable example — the same mapping the script applies, run on four
made-up Census rows (we cannot pull the raw ACS at render time; see the network
caveat below).  Compare the *coded* row a model would never want to ingest with
the *decoded* row we actually ship:

::: {#tbl-decode .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# A tiny, HAND-BUILT illustration of the real decode in download_credit_data.py.
# These are made-up Census codes (we don't pull raw ACS here) decoded with the
# exact same rules the script uses, so the "before/after" is honest.

# --- the real mapping fragments, copied from scripts/download_credit_data.py ---
OCC_RANGES = [
    (10, 960, "Management/Business/Finance"),
    (1005, 1980, "Computing/Engineering/Science"),
    (2001, 2920, "Education/Legal/Arts/Social"),
    (3000, 3655, "Healthcare"),
    (3700, 4655, "Service (food/clean/care/protective)"),
    (4700, 4965, "Sales"),
    (5000, 5940, "Office & Admin"),
    (6005, 9760, "Blue-collar (build/repair/prod/transport)"),
]
def occ_group(code: int) -> str:  # OCCP code → readable family (else Military/Other)
    return next((n for lo, hi, n in OCC_RANGES if lo <= code <= hi), "Military/Other")

# four made-up *coded* ACS rows (the integer vector the survey actually returns)
coded = pd.DataFrame({
    "SEX":   [1,      2,      1,      2],       # 1 = male, 2 = female
    "PINCP": [82000,  31000,  47000,  64000],   # personal income, dollars
    "OCCP":  [120,    3500,   6300,   2100],     # Census occupation code
})

# apply the SAME decode rules the script uses
decoded = pd.DataFrame({
    "sex":         (coded.SEX == 1).astype(int),          # 1 = male, 0 = female
    "income_high": (coded.PINCP > 50_000).astype(int),    # target = 𝟙[PINCP > $50k]
    "occupation":  coded.OCCP.map(occ_group),             # code range → family
})

print("coded ACS row (what the survey returns):")
print(coded.to_string(index=False))
print("\ndecoded row (what we ship):")
print(decoded.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
coded ACS row (what the survey returns):
 SEX  PINCP  OCCP
   1  82000   120
   2  31000  3500
   1  47000  6300
   2  64000  2100

decoded row (what we ship):
 sex  income_high                                occupation
   1            1               Management/Business/Finance
   0            0                                Healthcare
   1            0 Blue-collar (build/repair/prod/transport)
   0            1               Education/Legal/Arts/Social
```
:::
:::


Read row by row: code `OCCP=120` lands in `10–960` → *Management/Business/Finance*;
`OCCP=3500` lands in `3000–3655` → *Healthcare*; `PINCP=47000` is **below** the
cut so `income_high=0` even though `PINCP=82000` and `PINCP=64000` clear it; and
`SEX=2` becomes `sex=0`.  Every readable column in §1 is one of these lookups.

### 4b · The ACSIncome Filter — which survey rows survive

The raw ACS person file includes children, the unemployed, and people with no
reported wage — rows the income task is not about.  **ACSIncome** screens them out
with four conditions (from the script's `_acsincome_filter`):

| Census field | Condition | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `AGEP` | `> 16` | working-age (drops children) |
| `PINCP` | `> 100` | has reported personal income |
| `WKHP` | `> 0` | reports usual hours worked (employed) |
| `PWGTP` | `>= 1` | has a valid Census person-weight |

Conceptually the pipeline is **raw survey rows → filtered → decoded → sampled**:
the millions of raw California person-records shrink to the employed working-age
panel, get decoded into the readable columns, and are finally sampled down to a
fixed **30,000-row** panel with `random_state=0`.  We do not re-run this at render
time — the raw pull needs network and we only ship the processed
`credit_acs.csv` — but the committed counts are deterministic, and the loaded
panel is exactly its endpoint:

::: {#tbl-filter-effect .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# We can't re-run the raw download here, but we CAN confirm the endpoint: the
# loaded panel is the sampled, decoded result of that raw → filtered → sampled
# pipeline. (The raw/filtered counts below are illustrative of the funnel shape.)
funnel = pd.DataFrame({
    "stage": ["raw CA person rows", "after ACSIncome filter", "decoded + sampled (shipped)"],
    "rows":  ["~380,000 (needs network)", "~190,000 (needs network)", f"{len(credit):,}"],
})
print(funnel.to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nloaded panel columns: {list(credit.columns)}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
                      stage                     rows
         raw CA person rows ~380,000 (needs network)
     after ACSIncome filter ~190,000 (needs network)
decoded + sampled (shipped)                   30,000

loaded panel columns: ['age', 'education_years', 'hours_per_week', 'occupation', 'marital', 'sex', 'income_high']
```
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why the raw counts are quoted, not computed
The first two funnel rows need the live ACS pull (no network at render time), so
they are quoted as the funnel's *shape*, not recomputed.  The **shipped** row is
the real, loaded length — the deterministic endpoint of the committed script.
:::

The committed script is
[`scripts/download_credit_data.py`](../../scripts/download_credit_data.py); its
core is:

```python
# scripts/download_credit_data.py (excerpt — runs once, needs network)
from folktables import ACSDataSource
src  = ACSDataSource(survey_year="2018", horizon="1-Year", survey="person")
data = src.get_data(states=["CA"], download=True)        # US Census ACS
df   = acsincome_filter(data)                            # working-age, employed
out  = decode(df).sample(30_000, random_state=0)         # readable cols, fixed seed
out.to_csv("data/processed/credit_acs.csv")
```

As with the market data, we don't re-download at render time (CI has no network);
the result is committed as `data/processed/credit_acs.csv` and loaded with
`datasets.load_credit()`.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Real, and Cited
This is genuine US Census microdata, not a synthetic stand-in.  Sources:

- **American Community Survey** — US Census Bureau ([overview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Community_Survey)).
- **ACSIncome / folktables** — Ding, Hardt, Miller & Schmidt, *Retiring Adult: New Datasets for Fair Machine Learning*, NeurIPS 2021 ([arXiv:2108.04884](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.04884)).

The numbers above are deterministic for the committed state, year, and seed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Deliverable This Sets Up
The [fairness](../fairness/index.qmd) chapter trains a scorecard on the proxies
*with `sex` dropped*, shows the gap leaks anyway (chiefly through `occupation`),
then neutralises it — reporting the gap before and after.  Every number it quotes
traces back to this table.
:::

## What the Labs Reload From Here

This chapter is the **single home** for the fairness preprocessing.  The fairness
labs do not re-derive the decode or the ACSIncome filter — they reload the
**prepared** data this page produces and split it into the three pieces every
fairness method needs: the **target** `y` (`income_high`), the **protected
attribute** `s` (`sex`), and the **proxy feature matrix** `X` with `sex`
**dropped**.  Copy-paste this exact cell:

::: {#tbl-handoff .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
credit = datasets.load_credit()
y = credit["income_high"]                              # target: 1 if income > $50k
s = credit["sex"]                                      # protected: 1 = male
X = credit.drop(columns=["income_high", "sex"])        # proxies — sex DROPPED

print("X columns (proxies, sex dropped):", list(X.columns))
print(X.head(3).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\ny  rate (high-income)  : {y.mean():.0%}")
print(f"s  rate (male)         : {s.mean():.0%}")

# sex is gone from X, but occupation still recovers it:
# proxy leak: leak_acc = mean(guess == s),  guess = 𝟙[P(male | occupation) > 0.5]
occ_male = X.assign(sex=s).groupby("occupation").sex.transform("mean")   # P(male | occupation)
leak_acc = ((occ_male > 0.5).astype(int) == s).mean()                    # acc = mean(guess == s)
print(f"\nrecap: sex dropped from X, yet occupation alone recovers s "
      f"{leak_acc:.0%} of the time — the proxy leak survives the drop.")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
X columns (proxies, sex dropped): ['age', 'education_years', 'hours_per_week', 'occupation', 'marital']
 age  education_years  hours_per_week                  occupation       marital
  62               13              40              Office & Admin       Married
  33               16              65                       Sales       Married
  33               16              40 Management/Business/Finance Never married

y  rate (high-income)  : 41%
s  rate (male)         : 53%

recap: sex dropped from X, yet occupation alone recovers s 65% of the time — the proxy leak survives the drop.
```
:::
:::


`X` carries the proxies (`age`, `education_years`, `hours_per_week`,
`occupation`, `marital`); `y` is the label; `s` is the attribute we score
fairness against.  The printed recap is the crux of the whole module: dropping
`sex` from `X` does **not** remove `sex` from the data, because `occupation`
still carries it.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Lab Contract
The fairness labs **reload this prepared `(X, y, s)`** with the one-line recipe
above and do **not** re-derive the decode or the ACSIncome filter — that
preprocessing lives here, once.  The single allowed lab-specific extra step is
**encoding the categoricals** (one-hot `occupation` and `marital`) as each lab's
own modelling choice, since different methods want different encodings.  The
consuming labs are:

- [Tool 1 · drop-and-leak](../fairness/labs/lab-tool1-drop.qmd) — drops `sex`,
  shows `occupation` leaks it anyway.
- [Tool 2 · CKA penalty](../fairness/labs/lab-tool2-cka-penalty.qmd) — penalises
  the dependence between the score and `s`.
- [Job B · neutralise credit](../fairness/labs/lab-jobB-neutralize-credit.qmd) —
  the end-to-end neutralisation reporting the gap before and after.
:::
